sections.title: Abstract

summary.text: Abstract. LLM routers that decide from the task description alone inherit a Bayes-error floor in multi-turn agentic software engineering, because a similar issue can hide a one-line typo or a multi-module refactor. The paper proposes SWE-Router: a cheap model runs a few exploratory turns, and the router reads that partial trajectory before deciding whether to continue cheaply or escalate to an expensive model. A Bayes-optimality theorem says conditioning on the partial trajectory never harms routing and is strictly better when exploration is informative. Across weak/strong model pairs the authors report large cost-efficiency gains while keeping most of the strong model's performance, and they release a multi-LLM trajectory dataset.

sections.extract: Large language models (LLMs) embedded in multi-turn agentic harnesses are reshaping soft- ware engineering (SWE), but routing every task to a frontier model is wasteful when many issues admit cheap fixes. sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduction, opening. LLMs in agentic harnesses reach state-of-the-art resolution rates on repository-scale coding benchmarks, but their per-task cost exceeds open-weight alternatives by an order of magnitude or more while only a minority of tasks need frontier capability, so sending every task to a frontier model is wasteful. The block also carries the author affiliations (UCL, UNIST, PSL, Basel) and the venue line: the 5th Deep Learning for Code Workshop, ICML 2026.

sections.title: LLM Routing

summary.text: Introduction: LLM routing. Existing routers choose a model per instance as classifiers or calibrated probability estimators over the task description q, picking the cheapest model with the best cost-adjusted success probability. The authors argue this fits agentic SWE poorly, since the difficulty is often not identifiable from q alone; the disambiguating information is produced by the agent itself, whose ReAct-style turns spend much effort on bug localization and yield failed tests, file contents and stack traces that no prompt-only router can see.

sections.title: Value-Based Temporal Routing

summary.text: Introduction: value-based temporal routing and contributions. A cheap weak model m1 runs a few exploratory turns, then a learned value head, supervised by binary trajectory rewards and related to execution-free reward models, predicts from the partial trajectory whether m1 will solve the task; above a cost-adjusted threshold m1 continues, otherwise the task escalates to a stronger m2. Stated contributions: identifying the Bayes-error floor of prompt-conditioned routers and introducing temporal routing; SWE-Router as the first routing framework conditioned on the agent's own intermediate observations; and substantial cost reductions at matched resolution on SWE-Bench Verified against prompt-only baselines.

sections.title: Multi-turn Trajectories in Agentic Tasks

summary.text: Background and method. A SWE-agent trajectory is a sequence of (thought, action, observation) turns ending in a submit whose git patch is scored by unit tests as a binary reward. A binary router invokes the weak model m1 when its estimated success minus λ times its cost exceeds the strong model's; λ converts cost to success-probability units and tracing it gives the cost–quality Pareto curve. Because early turns reveal what the issue text lacks, the paper runs m1 for K turns, trains a value function (a pretrained LLM with a small classification head, cross-entropy on the binary reward) on that partial trajectory, and escalates by restarting m2 from q, with the K weak turns counted in the cost. Two simplifications reduce the rule to one tuned threshold; the authors use the one-sided version, continue iff r̂1 ≥ λ''.

sections.title: Theoretical Results

summary.text: Theoretical results. Routing is treated as a one-step Bayesian decision, so the Bayes-optimal expected utility is monotone in the information conditioned on (the classical "information never hurts" principle of DeGroot and Blackwell). Theorem 4.1: because the task description Q is a function of the partial trajectory S_t, the optimal utility given S_t is at least that given Q, strictly better whenever the expected utility gap given S_t is not determined by Q. The proof sketch uses max{a,b} = ½(a+b+|a−b|), the tower rule and conditional Jensen. Read practically, prompt-only routers see only the gap averaged over Q, while a few exploratory turns let easy instances stay cheap and hard ones escalate; the gain vanishes only when the prompt already determines the choice.

sections.extract: Viewing routing as a one-step Bayesian decision problem, the Bayes-optimal expected utility is monotone in the conditioning σ-algebra. This is the classical “information never hurts” principle for Bayes decision rules (DeGroot, 1962; Blackwell, 1953), instantiated in our trajectory- conditioning setting. sections.title: Evaluation Metrics

summary.text: Evaluation metrics and Algorithm 1. AUROC scores the value head as a binary classifier of success; Route-AUC is the normalised area under the cost-versus-resolved-rate curve from sweeping the threshold, with all-weak at (0,0) and all-strong at (1,1), so 0 is cost-proportional interpolation and 1 is the strong model's resolved rate at the weak model's cost. Algorithm 1 gives the deployment procedure: run m1 for up to K steps (returning early if it submits), score the trajectory with the value head, then either continue with m1 to submission or restart m2 from q.

sections.title: Experiment Setting

summary.text: Experiment setting and start of results. Training and test splits come from SWE-Smith and SWE-Bench, validation from SWE-Smith only. Trajectories are generated in mini-SWE-agent, forming two weak/strong pairs: gpt-5-mini or deepseek-v3.2 as the weak model and gemini-3-pro-preview as the strong one. The value head is Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with a two-class head fine-tuned by LoRA. Baselines are logistic regression, k-NN and XGBoost on text-embedding-3-large embeddings of q, plus the authors' own non-temporal router (K=0). The block includes the text of Figure 2, cost-versus-resolved curves on held-out SWE-Bench Verified against a random-assignment band from 400 Monte-Carlo permutations; its caption says SWE-Router (K=3) lies above the band and for some thresholds exceeds the strong-model endpoint.

sections.title: Does conditioning on the partial trajectory improve over prompt-only baselines?

summary.text: Results: does conditioning on the partial trajectory beat prompt-only baselines? The authors read Figure 2 as SWE-Router lying above the random band for both pairs and dominating the embedding baselines over most of the cost range. On the SWE-Bench Verified test split, with deepseek-v3.2 as m1 SWE-Router reaches Route-AUC 0.780, +15.3 points over the non-temporal K=0 router, and with gpt-5-mini as m1 it is +12 points over the strongest baseline. AUROC is not strongly correlated with routing performance. On both pairs the curve briefly passes above the all-strong point, which the authors attribute to weak and strong models solving different subsets of instances.

sections.title: Related Work

summary.text: Related work, short form. Agentic frameworks such as ReAct and SWE-agent let LLMs work on real repositories, and code benchmarks have moved from self-contained problems to repository-level evaluation led by SWE-bench and its curated subset. FrugalGPT introduced cost-aware cascades and RouteLLM formalised binary routing from preference data. All of these condition on the prompt alone; SWE-Router differs by conditioning on the partial agent trajectory.

sections.title: Conclusion

summary.text: Conclusion. SWE-Router routes on a short partial trajectory of a cheap weak model rather than the task description alone; Theorem 4.1 shows this never harms routing and helps when exploration is informative. Evaluated on two popular model pairs, it improves Route-AUC by at least 12 points over the strongest baseline on the SWE-Bench Verified test split.

sections.extract: We introduced SWE-Router, a value-based routing framework that conditions on a short partial trajectory of a cheap weak model rather than on the task description alone. A simple Bayes-optimality result (Theorem 4.1) shows that this conditioning never harms routing and is strictly better when exploration is informative. sections.title: Impact Statement

summary.text: Impact statement. The authors expect lower frontier-model inference cost and energy use at little performance cost, but warn that routing on partial trajectories could be misused to bypass safety-focused frontier models, and name routing that also weighs task safety as future work.

sections.extract: Our approach provides a clear positive impact of reduced frontier-model inference cost and energy use with minimal tradeoff in the overall performance. However, our proposed approach of utilizing partial trajectories can be misused to bypass safety-focused frontier models for malicious pur- poses. sections.title: Data Collection

summary.text: Appendix: data collection. Because SWE-smith ships only claude-3.7-sonnet trajectories, the authors generated and release their own. SWE-smith is sub-sampled into repository-disjoint train (about 1.7k trajectories per weak model), validation (about 210, for threshold tuning) and test (about 170–346) partitions, labelled by the SWE-smith unit tests. Trajectories were also collected on all 500 SWE-bench Verified issues for all models; under the mix-1 constitution four fifths of these go to training, so the genuinely held-out SWE-bench slice is 100 instances.

sections.title: Experiment Designs

summary.text: Appendix: experiment design. Mix-1 merges SWE-Smith training trajectories with four of five cross-validation folds of SWE-Bench Verified; validation comes from SWE-Smith, with separate test splits from SWE-Smith and SWE-Bench Verified. The LoRA adapter uses r=32, α=64, dropout 0.05; training is 5 epochs, learning rate 5×10⁻⁵ cosine with 50 warmup steps, effective batch 16 and an 8192-token context. One packed row per trajectory applies the head at every user-turn boundary K from 0 to Kmax=4, and each q is replaced by a random one of three LLM paraphrases during training and validation. The baselines repeat those of the main text.

sections.title: Proof of Theorem 4.1

summary.text: Appendix: full proof of Theorem 4.1. With Δ = U1 − U2, the max identity writes the Bayes-optimal utility as a Z-independent term plus ½E|E[Δ|Z]|. Since Q is a function of S_t, the tower property and conditional Jensen with |x| give E|E[Δ|Q]| ≤ E|E[Δ|S_t]|, so V(S_t) ≥ V(Q), with equality iff E[Δ|S_t] is σ(Q)-measurable, that is, iff the partial trajectory says nothing about Δ beyond the prompt.

sections.title: Additional Related Work

summary.text: Appendix: additional related work in three groups. LLMs for software engineering: OpenHands, structure-aware and two-stage repair, planning, multi-agent testing and executable code actions, with SWE-smith and Agent-RLVR for training and SWE-RM for execution-free patch scoring, to which the value head is related. SWE benchmarks: cross-file completion, tool use, SWE-bench and its multimodal, multilingual, higher-rigor, live and performance variants, with contamination concerns answered by contamination-resistant benchmarks and SWE-bench Pro. LLM routing: hybrid, mixing, meta-modelling and ensembling approaches, contrastive, classification, graph and budget-aware routers, reasoning-mode routing and cascades, model embeddings for unseen models, RL-based routers, and routing benchmarks.
